summary: Help children aged 4–6 grasp the cardinality principle: the last number word said when counting a set tells how many objects there are (its total), and that total does not change when the objects are rearranged or counted in a different order. This is the bridge from counting-as-reciting to counting-as-quantity and underpins +1/−1, comparison and early addition/subtraction. Useful checks include 'how many?' answered without recounting, 'give me exactly N', and arrangement/order-invariance probes.
misconceptions: Recounting when asked 'how many?' — treating the count as a performance rather than something that yields a total (the diagnostic error).
Last-word parroting without meaning — repeating the final word said even when the count started at the wrong number (Bermejo: counts 5 from 'three', answers 'seven').
Believing rearranging or spreading out a set changes how many there are (pre-conservation; length/spacing mistaken for quantity).
Thinking the last number names only the last OBJECT, not the whole set.

activities.title: Count, scatter, re-ask: the total that stays put
steps: Count a small set of objects aloud (start with 5, e.g. five toy ducks or cars) and say the total: '…four, five — five altogether!'
Place or keep visible a total badge/numeral card showing the count beside the set.
Now move the same objects around: bunch them in a corner, spread them out in a ring or long line — without adding or removing any.

Before recounting, say how many there are now and explain why (if the total card is still showing, ask why the card still matches the set, so the answer is reasoned rather than simply read off the card).
Check by recounting together only if needed, and notice the total is the same.
activities.insight: Moving objects around cannot change how many there are; the total is a fixed property of the set, so you do not need to recount after rearranging.

activities.title: Give me exactly N (count-out task)
steps: From a heap or big box of objects, count out exactly a requested number (e.g. 'give me exactly 5 cars', 'give me exactly 4').
Stop as soon as the requested amount is reached, rather than counting the whole heap.
Check the handed-over set by recounting together.
activities.insight: A number word is a stop-signal for a specific quantity: knowing 'five' means being able to produce a set of exactly five, not just reciting up to five.

activities.title: Start counting from three (parroting trap)
steps: Lay out 5 objects. The adult asks the child to count them but to START saying 'three' on the first object, then 'four', 'five', 'six', 'seven'.
Afterwards ask: 'So how many objects are there really?'
Discuss why the answer is still five even though the last word said was 'seven'.
activities.insight: The correct total (five) is a property of the set, not just whatever word you happen to say last; answering 'seven' may mean the child is repeating the last word rather than finding how many (or may reflect confusion about the unusual instruction).

activities.title: Count from the other end (order-irrelevance)
steps: Count a line of objects left-to-right and say the total.
Count the same line right-to-left (or starting from a middle object) and say the total again.
Compare: as long as each object is counted exactly once, the total is the same whichever object you start from and whatever order you count in.
activities.insight: The total does not depend on which object you count first or the order you count in.

activities.title: Subitising small sets as wholes
steps: Briefly show dot cards, dice faces, domino patterns or a five-frame (or a ten-frame filled only partly) showing small quantities (≤5) and say how many without counting one-by-one.
Match a numeral card to a set to link the symbol to the quantity.
Use the 'count → cover it → how many?' routine: count a set, cover it, then recall the total from memory instead of recounting.
activities.insight: Small quantities can be recognised instantly as whole amounts, reinforcing that a number names an amount, and the total can be recalled rather than re-derived.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: will bunching change how many? (assessment companion)
steps: Show 5 cars in a line and agree there are 5.
Before anything is moved, PREDICT: 'If I bunch these into a pile, will there be more, fewer, or the same — and why?' Commit to a reason first.
Then bunch them and count together to check against the prediction.
Afterwards answer: 'How could you have known it would still be 5 without counting?'
activities.insight: The reason given before observing reveals understanding: 'the same, because you didn't add or take any' shows conservation; 'fewer, it's a smaller pile' does not.

checkQuestion: Here are 5 toy cars in a row. Count them for me. (Child counts to 5.) Good — so how many cars are there? Now watch, I'll bunch them into a pile. Without counting again, how many cars are in the pile now — and how do you know?
checkAnswer: Still 5 — I already counted them and I didn't add any or take any away, so bunching them up doesn't change how many.
